name: Optimization and Training Procedures
text:
# Optimization and Training Procedures

Also called: NeRF Optimization, Radiance Field Training

## Overview
This article details the specific optimization loops, hyperparameter configurations, and training strategies used to converge [Neural Radiance Fields](#4972-neural-radiance-fields.md) (NeRFs) and their variants. It addresses the problem of efficiently minimizing the photometric reconstruction error between rendered images and ground truth views. It differs from sibling articles by focusing exclusively on the *process* of learning (optimizers, schedules, initialization) rather than the *architecture* of the network or the *mathematics* of volume rendering itself.

## Shared principles
The optimization of NeRF-based models generally follows a stochastic gradient descent framework. The objective function is typically the [Mean Squared Error](#1651-mse-loss-and-psnr-conversion.md) (MSE) between the rendered color $\hat{C}$ and the ground truth color $C$ for a batch of rays:
$$
\mathcal{L} = \sum_{r \in \text{batch}} \| \hat{C}(r) - C(r) \|^2
$$
Gradients are computed via backpropagation through the [differentiable volume rendering](#43-differentiable-volume-rendering.md) integral. The choice of optimizer (typically Adam or AdamW) and learning rate schedule is critical for converging to a local minimum that represents the 3D scene accurately.

## Subtopics

### [Activation-Informed Coarse-to-Fine Rendering](12277-activation-informed-coarse-to-fine-rendering.md)
This method accelerates inference by conditionally skipping the expensive fine-pass MLP evaluation based on intermediate activation values from the coarse pass [12277-activation-informed-coarse-to-fine-rendering.md]. It differs from standard coarse-to-fine rendering by using a conditional mask derived from network internals (activations) rather than fixed density thresholds or sampling strategies. It is chosen when inference speed is prioritized over the marginal quality gain of the fine pass for background rays.

### [Last Layer Re-training](13532-last-layer-re-training.md)
[Last Layer Re-training](#13532-last-layer-re-training.md) propagates a color edit from a single view to a pre-trained [NeRF](#1185-nerf-neural-radiance-fields.md) by selectively retraining only the last layer of the color MLP [13532-last-layer-re-training.md]. It differs from full re-training by preserving the geometric and view-dependent information encoded in deeper layers, enabling near real-time editing. It is chosen for interactive editing tasks where global consistency must be maintained with minimal computational overhead.

### Rip-NeRF Optimization
Rip-NeRF optimization involves learning the tiny MLP weights and the ripmaps $R$. Model weights are initialized following Glorot and Bengio (2010), while ripmaps $R$ start from a uniform distribution over $[-0.01, 0.01]$ [S1]. The optimizer is AdamW [S1]. The base learning rate is $2 \times 10^{-3}$, scaled by 10x for $R$ due to its direct scene representation role [S1]. The learning rate schedule reduces the rate by 0.6x at steps 60K, 90K, 100K, and 108K, over a total of 120K iterations [S1]. The batch size is dynamically adjusted to maintain approximately 256K spheres per batch [S1].

## Background
The [standard NeRF training](#985-nerf-training-loop-with-random-ray-batching.md) procedure was introduced by Mildenhall et al. in 2020 [S6, unofficial], using Adam with a fixed learning rate. Subsequent works like [Instant-NGP](#6604-instant-ngp.md) [Müller et al. 2022] introduced [hash grids](#936-hash-grids.md) and adaptive batch sizing. Rip-NeRF [S1] introduced specific initialization and scheduling for its ripmap-based representation.

## Sources
